analysis.one_liner: Lets gun violence victims sue gun makers and sellers, undoing the law that shields them.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in June 2023 with 29 Senate cosponsors, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee and died there when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently bars most civil lawsuits against gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade groups when a gun is later used unlawfully. This bill would repeal that shield, letting victims and their families sue in court, and would make ATF gun-trace data usable as evidence in those cases. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: People shot or injured by guns, and families of victims, would regain the right to sue manufacturers, dealers, and trade associations over how guns were made, marketed, or sold. Cities and states could also pursue suits, and plaintiffs would be able to use ATF trace data to show where crime guns came from.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun violence victims and their families

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which prohibits civil actions against firearm or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations for damages from criminal or unlawful misuse of a firearm [S2] [S3].

Makes the ATF Firearms Trace System database subject to subpoena and discovery and admissible as evidence in civil actions and administrative proceedings, on the same basis as other information [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Gun manufacturers, dealers, importers, and their trade associations would face civil lawsuits and litigation costs, and potentially damages, that current law blocks. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers through prices or reduced product availability.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the liability shield would expose lawful manufacturers and dealers to lawsuits over third-party criminal acts, which the industry argues could push small dealers out of business and raise the cost of firearms for lawful buyers [S2].
Opening the ATF trace database to civil discovery would release law-enforcement-sensitive data into litigation, a change that raises privacy and investigative concerns beyond the courtroom.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give shooting victims and their families a legal avenue they were denied by a 2005 law, and trace data could strengthen those cases. The cost falls on the gun industry, whose lawful dealers could face suits over conduct that was legal at the time of sale; some of that cost would likely reach gun buyers through prices. The design is a straightforward liability rule change; the trade-off is industry litigation exposure versus victim access to court.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Introduced June 20, 2023 by Sen. Blumenthal with 26 original cosponsors, and read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day [S1] [S5].
It gathered 29 cosponsors, all Democrats plus one Independent, but no further action was ever listed: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote [S4] [S5].
The bill died in committee at the end of the 118th Congress [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and their trade associations remain shielded from most civil lawsuits, exactly as before; victims and their families are no better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and dealers, still lawsuit-proof

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee

for.name: Gun violence prevention groups
for.what_they_did: Have long pushed Congress to repeal the industry's liability shield

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill: no hearing, no markup, no vote, letting it die at the end of the Congress

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Did not bring the bill to the Senate floor at any point in the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 29 cosponsors were 28 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 4 Senate independents, with no Republican support; the bill died in committee without a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill died, so the industry keeps the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act shield that blocks most civil suits over criminal misuse of its products, including suits that might be supported by ATF trace data. Victims keep the burden of their losses.
The bill would have repealed the shield for trade associations as well; its death preserves their protected status under current law.
